html:
The only stock exchange in Israel, opened in Tel Aviv in 1953. Israelis call it the Bursa.

Its forerunner was a securities exchange office set up by a bank in 1935, under the British mandate. In the early decades of the state the economy was dominated by the government, the labour federation and a few big banks, and trading was thin.

A crisis hit in 1983. Israel's big banks had for years propped up the price of their own shares. When the scheme broke, bank shares collapsed, the exchange closed for over two weeks, and the state took over the banks. Reform followed, along with the end of the high inflation of the early 1980s.

From the 1990s Israel's technology industry boomed, fed by army research and universities like the Technion. Many of its firms chose to list on Nasdaq in New York, but the exchange grew too, and some companies list in both places. In 2019 the exchange became a listed company on its own market.
sum: The only stock exchange in Israel, opened in Tel Aviv in 1953. Israelis call it the Bursa.
